children: Boeing

shares plunged 10% Tuesday to an 18-month low after Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg warned that the aircraft manufacturer would take longer than expected to increase production of its best-selling 737 Max jets, threatening aircraft deliveries and future cash flow.
The company now expects to reach a production rate of 47 737 jets a month in early 2027, rather than this year. The delay means Boeing
won't meet its previous target of delivering 500 commercial aircraft in 2026, Ortberg said in an interview with CNBC.
Investors also were disappointed by the company's cash flow outlook. Boeing

expects to generate approximately $3 billion in free cash flow in 2027 and $6 billion in 2028. Those figures fall well short of Wall Street consensus estimates of $5.6 billion and $9.6 billion, respectively, based on LSEG data.
The warnings overshadowed Boeing's

third-quarter results, which showed sharply narrower losses, positive free cash flow and a record $745 billion order backlog. The company reported an adjusted loss of $0.34 a share, missing analysts' consensus estimate for a loss of $0.20 a share by $0.14.
Revenue increased 4% to $24.19 billion from $23.27 billion a year earlier, missing Wall Street expectations by $180 million.
For investors, the selloff highlights a persistent problem in Boeing's

turnaround: Strong demand for aircraft doesn't necessarily translate into near-term profits or cash generation. The company must increase production without repeating the quality-control failures that contributed to years of regulatory scrutiny, delivery disruptions and financial losses.
Production delays threaten recovery
Boeing

had previously planned to reach its target production rate of 47 737 jets a month during the summer. However, manufacturing constraints have slowed progress, including difficulties producing enough wings to support higher assembly rates.
Ortberg acknowledged the pressure to accelerate production but emphasized the importance of avoiding another round of manufacturing problems.
"We are ramping up aircraft, and we're doing that in the right way," Ortberg told CNBC.
The company continues to face production challenges involving its 787 Dreamliner and 777 freighter programs.
The delays are particularly consequential because deliveries of 737 Max aircraft are a major source of cash for Boeing
. Slower output can postpone customer payments while the company continues spending on suppliers, employees and factory operations.
Boeing
delivered 161 commercial aircraft during the third quarter, compared with 160 a year earlier. Its Commercial Airplanes division generated $10.72 billion in revenue, down 3% from the prior year.

The division reported an operating loss of $697 million, substantially narrower than its $5.35 billion loss a year earlier. Its operating margin improved to negative 6.5% from negative 48.3%, although higher production and supply chain costs continued to weigh on profitability.
Quarterly loss narrows
Boeing's
net loss narrowed to $116 million, or $0.26 a share, from $5.34 billion, or $7.14 a share, a year earlier.
The company reported operating earnings of $354 million, compared with an operating loss of $4.78 billion in the year-earlier quarter.

Operating cash flow rose 33% to $1.5 billion, while free cash flow increased to $464 million from $238 million. The latest quarter included approximately $700 million in payments related to a Department of Justice settlement.
Despite the improvement, the weaker multiyear cash flow outlook raised concerns about how quickly Boeing
can strengthen its balance sheet and reduce its substantial debt burden.
The company ended September with $20.7 billion in cash and marketable securities and $45.9 billion in consolidated debt.
Defense and services businesses show strength
Boeing's
Defense, Space & Security business provided a brighter spot, with revenue increasing 15% to $7.94 billion.

Operating earnings climbed to $492 million from $114 million, lifting the division's operating margin to 6.2% from 1.7%. The improvement included a $252 million gain from the sale of HRL Laboratories.

During the quarter, the company was selected by the U.S. Navy to design and build the F/A-XX next-generation fighter aircraft. It also secured a seven-year contract to expand production of PAC-3 missile seekers.
Global Services revenue increased 4% to $5.57 billion, while operating earnings rose 9% to $1.02 billion. The division's operating margin improved to 18.3% from 17.5%.
Boeing

also achieved important certification milestones. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the 737-7 during the third quarter and the larger 737-10 in October. The company continues to target its first 777-9 delivery in 2027.
Record backlog meets slower execution
Boeing's
total backlog reached a record $745 billion, including more than 6,300 commercial aircraft valued at approximately $612 billion.
That order book provides substantial long-term revenue potential, supported by airline demand for fuel-efficient aircraft and government spending on military equipment.
However, the company's latest production and cash flow forecasts suggest that converting those orders into revenue and profits will take longer than investors anticipated.
In a memo to employees following the earnings announcement, Ortberg acknowledged the company's progress while emphasizing the work ahead.

"Expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg wrote. "We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day."
For investors, the question is no longer whether Boeing

has sufficient demand for its aircraft. It's whether the manufacturer can overcome persistent production constraints quickly enough to generate the cash needed to support its recovery and reduce debt.

title: Boeing stock plunges to 18-mth low on production delays, cash flow outlook
